doc.title: David Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 18, 2003

title: Playing with the Grateful Dead
summary: Meeting Bob Weir through a Satchel Paige musical, sitting in at Madison Square Garden, Jerry Garcia, and his jazz album of Dead music.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: I wanted to briefly just ask you about your experience with the Grateful Dead.

Oh well, you know, God, first of all Bob Weir is really a good friend of mine. And the way we met was through Michael Nash and Carrie Williams. They asked me to be part of this — of writing the music for a musical about Satchel Paige. And so we began to collaborate, Taj Mahal, Bob Weir and myself, Michael Nash and Carrie were writing the libretto. And it’s been a process now that’s been going on for seven years you know. And I think — we’ve had several workshops, we had Avery Brooks come in and direct us, we’ve had several directors coming in to do workshops. And I think maybe approaching ten years, it’s going to eventually be out there on Broadway. We have 35 songs, and what we’ve realized ourselves, it’s pretty good songwriting. I think the music is far ahead of the script. And they’re doing revisions of the script. And this brought me into the idea of like them saying well hey David, we’re playing at Madison Square Garden, why don’t you come and sit in. Well all right, I’ll sit in, I’ll be down. So I come and sit in. Bamm it’s like twenty thousand people there. And I’d never seen such an attentive audience. I mean I play, I’ve played the Vanguard and this jazz club and that, the Blue Note and all this, there’s always somebody talking at the bar that I can hear, usually a musician you know. And I play, I say waaa on my sax and I see all the heads. Wow. They’re with me the whole time. What a wonderful audience these guys have developed. And I was just thinking man, I wish we had such a dedicated crew, especially twenty thousand of them you know. So then I go sit in with them out in San Francisco. Same thing. And then I played one other time with them. And I played with Jerry Garcia’s band, I sat in with him at the Madison Square Garden and that was a gas too, because this guy was fantastic.

Then he dies, right in the middle of his time, and it’s just incredible that, I mean I never got paid a dime to play with them but what I did get was all this recognition from all these people. Every time I played a concert, somebody would come in with a shirt like this and say, “Play one for Jerry, Dave.” You know, I’m like okay. And so then I did an album of their music. Because they were really such nice people. I was like well hey let me take your music and put it in a jazz thing, let’s put this together and let me put this with my octet and see what that would do. And it was a very successful album. People loved it. And after that I was like in their camp. So now the Dead is back together, Phil Lesh just got a new liver, they’re back in it man. Kreutzmann came back and Billy Hart, he’s back, and they had to have Kreutzmann because Billy, he could play a lot of things but time is not one of them. But now they’ve got Billy to play the time so now they’re really back. Because he had really retired. So that’s why they’re back, because Billy came back. And God bless them. I love those guys. I mean and the thing is, I went in a bookstore and they have all of these new books about Jerry Garcia. I counted like fourteen of them. And I’m on like several pages of every one of them, just because of those few situations that I just spoke of. And so it’s like a cult thing man. I will always be connected with these people. And we’re talking about doing some stuff now.
That’s great. You seem to have the most wide open ears I can imagine. Even—
